topic: definite integrals and the Fundamental Theorem: diagnosing bounds, sign and variable-of-integration errors

traps.desc: evaluated from the smaller bound to the larger one, ignoring that the given bounds run backwards
dropped the parentheses around the value at the lower bound, so only the first piece of it was subtracted
replaced the variable of integration with the upper bound instead of integrating, so the integrand itself was evaluated
subtracted the two given integrals but reported the result for the bounds in increasing order, leaving the sign unflipped
used positive cosine as the antiderivative of sine, which reverses the sign of the whole result
read off the integrand at the moving bound but forgot the minus sign that comes from the variable sitting at the lower bound
substituted a new variable but kept the original bounds, so the antiderivative in the new variable was evaluated at the old numbers

problems.desc: Open explanation: the student must explain why reversing the bounds of a definite integral negates it, why the letter used for the variable of integration cannot appear in the answer of a definite integral, and what goes wrong when a substitution changes the variable but not the bounds. Read the reasoning by hand; any argument grounded in the Fundamental Theorem's F(b) minus F(a) form, or in the dummy status of the integration variable, earns full credit.
